E052-01.notes: Object of preposition 'of' in a relative clause needs 'whom': 'Skaters, many of whom had paid for a full evening, spent...'. A 'who' is subject case after a preposition. B 'them' turns the interrupter into an independent clause wedged inside the main clause ('Skaters, many of them had paid..., spent') - ungrammatical. D 'many of whose had paid' - possessive with no noun, nonsensical.

E052-02.notes: 'Spending most of the 1940s on the problem.' is a fragment; D attaches it as a participial modifier: '...do the job alone, spending most of the 1940s on the problem.' B semicolon leaves a fragment after it. C 'decided to build... and spending' is faulty parallelism (no matching verb form; reads as if 'spending' pairs with 'decided').

E052-03.notes: 'which he finished in 1949' is a nonessential clause (his first successful model is already uniquely identified) and needs a pair of commas: 'His first successful model, which he finished in 1949, combined three tasks.' A has no commas (and 'which' without commas is nonstandard for a nonrestrictive clause). C and D each use only one of the two required commas, separating subject from verb or leaving the clause unclosed.

E052-04.notes: A colon after the independent clause 'combined three tasks' correctly introduces the list. B semicolon followed by a list (not an independent clause) is wrong. C 'such as:' puts a colon after a phrase that is not a complete clause, and 'such as' implies a partial list of examples although exactly three tasks are named. D 'tasks that were shaving the ice, washing it, and drying it' is awkward and illogical (tasks do not 'shave').

E052-05.notes: Only C quantifies the reduction (one driver vs. a crew; minutes vs. more than an hour), echoing sentence 3. A 'faster' is vague; B 'clear improvement' is general; D is about where it worked, not how much work was reduced. Consistent with the historical record (Zamboni's machine let one operator resurface in roughly 10-15 minutes).

E052-06.notes: Subject is singular 'Each'; the past-tense narrative ('bought') needs 'was': 'Each of the rinks that bought a machine was able to shorten...'. A 'were' and C 'have been' are plural; D 'are' is plural and shifts to present tense.

E052-07.notes: 'regardless of who made it' clarifies that the name is applied even to resurfacers made by other companies. A (naming of later models) and C (company stopped making resurfacers) are not in the phrase; B misreads it as a quality claim.

E052-08.notes: 'the figure skater Sonja Henie' is a restrictive appositive (the name identifies which of many figure skaters) so no punctuation: 'the figure skater Sonja Henie saw the machine...'. B paired commas would imply she was the only figure skater. C single comma splits the appositive from the subject-verb sequence ('the figure skater, Sonja Henie saw'). D single dash with no closing dash is likewise unbalanced.

E052-09.notes: Sentence 9 ('Within a few years, rinks across the country were placing orders') follows naturally from Henie's 1950 order (sentence 8) and sets up sentence 10, which refers to 'the rinks that bought a machine'. B before 8 breaks chronology (spread before the first outside order). C after 10 leaves 10's reference to rinks buying machines unsupported. D after 11 places it after the present-day conclusion.
